details:
**"The Tyger"**
Blake's most famous poem and the giveaway in nearly every question. It opens "Tyger Tyger, burning bright, / In the forests of the night" and asks "What immortal hand or eye / Could frame thy fearful symmetry?", wondering what "hammer," "chain," "furnace," and "anvil" could have made the beast; when "the stars threw down their spears / And water'd heaven with their tears," the speaker asks, "Did he smile his work to see? / Did he who made the Lamb make thee?"

**Songs of Innocence and of Experience**
Blake's 1794 combined collection of illustrated poems, showing "the two contrary states of the human soul." Many poems in the gentle Songs of Innocence (1789) have darker counterparts in Songs of Experience, as "The Lamb" is paired with "The Tyger"; Blake engraved, printed, and hand-colored the books himself.

**"The Lamb"**
The Songs of Innocence counterpart to "The Tyger," in which a child asks the lamb "Little Lamb who made thee / Dost thou know who made thee?" The creator gave the lamb "clothing of delight, / Softest clothing wooly bright" and a tender voice "Making all the vales rejoice," and the child answers that the maker is Christ, who "calls himself a Lamb," ending "Little Lamb God bless thee."

**"The Chimney Sweeper" (Songs of Innocence)**
A poem that begins "When my mother died I was very young," spoken by a boy sold into chimney sweeping before he "could scarcely cry 'weep!'" His friend Tom Dacre cries when his curly hair is shaved, then dreams of sweeps "lock'd up in coffins of black" whom an angel frees to run "down a green plain"; the poem ends with the sadly ironic line "So if all do their duty, they need not fear harm."

**"The Chimney Sweeper" (Songs of Experience)**
The bitter companion poem, which opens with "A little black thing among the snow, / Crying 'weep, 'weep, in notes of woe!" The child says his parents, because he was "happy upon the heath," "clothed me in the clothes of death" and have gone to church to praise "God & his Priest & King / Who make up a heaven of our misery."

**"London"**
A Songs of Experience poem in which the speaker wanders "thro' each charter'd street" and sees in every face "Marks of weakness, marks of woe," hearing "the mind-forg'd manacles." The chimney-sweeper's cry appalls "every blackning Church," "the hapless Soldiers sigh / Runs in blood down Palace walls," and "the youthful Harlots curse" blights "the Marriage hearse."

**"A Poison Tree"**
A Songs of Experience poem that begins "I was angry with my friend: / I told my wrath, my wrath did end. / I was angry with my foe: / I told it not, my wrath did grow." The speaker waters his anger with tears and suns it "with smiles, / And with soft deceitful wiles" until it bears "an apple bright," and in the morning he sees his foe "outstretch'd beneath the tree."

**"And did those feet in ancient time" ("Jerusalem")**
The short poem in the preface to Blake's epic Milton, asking whether Christ once walked in England and whether Jerusalem was built "Among these dark Satanic Mills." The speaker demands "Bring me my Bow of burning gold: / Bring me my Arrows of desire" and "my Chariot of fire"; set to music by Hubert Parry, it is now the hymn "Jerusalem."

**Milton: A Poem**
One of Blake's prophetic books, in which the spirit of the poet John Milton returns from eternity to correct his errors. Milton falls like a comet and enters the narrator's left foot, and his female counterpart Ololon, who appears as "a Virgin of twelve years," descends to find him.

**The Marriage of Heaven and Hell**
A satirical prose-and-verse work responding to the mystic Emanuel Swedenborg. It claims Milton "was a true Poet and of the Devil's party without knowing it," and its "Proverbs of Hell" include "The road of excess leads to the palace of wisdom," "Exuberance is Beauty," and "Drive your cart and your plow over the bones of the dead" (the source of Olga Tokarczuk's novel title); its line "If the doors of perception were cleansed" gave Aldous Huxley the title The Doors of Perception.

**"The Sick Rose"**
A short, enigmatic Songs of Experience poem beginning "O Rose thou art sick." An "invisible worm, / That flies in the night" finds the rose's bed of "crimson joy," and "his dark secret love / Does thy life destroy."

**The Four Zoas, Albion, Urizen, and Los**
Blake's private mythology, developed in his prophetic books such as Vala, or The Four Zoas. The primeval man Albion falls and splits into four Zoas: Urizen (reason), Luvah (passion), Tharmas (the senses), and Urthona, whose fallen form is Los, the blacksmith-like figure of imagination.

**Other prophetic books (America, Visions of the Daughters of Albion, Europe)**
In America a Prophecy, the fiery rebel Orc embodies the American Revolution, and in Visions of the Daughters of Albion, Oothoon is called "the soft soul of America." Blake's famous image The Ancient of Days, the frontispiece to Europe a Prophecy, shows the bearded Urizen reaching down with a compass to measure the world.

**"Earth's Answer"**
The second poem of Songs of Experience, replying to its "Introduction," which calls on Earth to wake. Earth "rais'd up her head / From the darkness dread & drear" and pleads, "Break this heavy chain, / That does freeze my bones around."

**Other Songs (The Clod and the Pebble, Infant Joy and Infant Sorrow, Lyca)**
In "The Clod and the Pebble," the clay clod describes a selfless love that "seeketh not itself to please" and builds "a Heaven in Hells despair," while the pebble praises a selfish love that "builds a Hell in Heavens despite." "Infant Joy" presents a two-day-old baby named Joy, while in "Infant Sorrow" a "bound and weary" baby "thought best / To sulk upon my mothers breast"; other clue poems include "The Little Girl Lost" and "The Little Girl Found" (about Lyca), "Holy Thursday," "The Fly" ("Am not I / A fly like thee?"), and "A Divine Image" ("Cruelty has a Human Heart / And Jealousy a Human Face").
